documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Separation of Standard Revision From Target Adjustment, a distinction among three ways a discrepancy can disappear. Someone can correct the account, change the situation the account describes, or revise the standard used to compare them. Each change can produce agreement at the next assessment. What that agreement tells us about the original account depends on how it came about. The paper sets out the evidence needed to identify each change. A correction requires grounds for judging that the revised account describes the situation more accurately. An adjustment requires evidence of what someone changed in the situation. A revision of the standard requires the earlier and later criteria, the grounds for the revision, and the authority under which it was made. Several changes can occur together. Recording each one allows people who rely on the account, or whose circumstances were adjusted, to examine what resolved the discrepancy and who can challenge that resolution. The paper places the distinction alongside Hasok Chang’s account of how standards of measurement improve and examines two documented cases. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union adopted a definition of a planet and, in a separate resolution, classified Pluto as a dwarf planet. The change in classification followed from the adopted criterion. Britain’s Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 made several changes together. It advanced the calendar from September 2 to September 14 in 1752, revised the rule for future leap years, and preserved the actual time due under existing agreements for rents and debts. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper offers a distinction for human–AI evaluation. Suppose an AI assistant lists a room as available while a tentative reservation blocks its use. A later check could find agreement because the assistant corrected its answer, the reservation holder released the room, or the booking policy changed to permit use during a tentative hold. Each history gives the evaluator different grounds for judging the assistant’s original answer.

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Simulated Likeness Substituted for Personal Endorsement, a structural constraint on what a recognizable voice, appearance, or manner can establish about a person’s assent. It distinguishes three questions. Who gave permission to create or use the likeness? What evidence shows that the person endorsed the particular words or action, or authorized that commitment in advance? What grounds support a judgment about what the person would have said or done? In 1997, a Dirt Devil commercial used footage of Fred Astaire dancing with a hat rack and replaced the rack with a vacuum cleaner. Astaire had performed the dance. The advertisement gave it a new purpose. His widow, Robyn Astaire, authorized the use and cited his earlier routines with household props as grounds for believing he would have approved. His daughter, Ava Astaire McKenzie, objected that the advertisement betrayed his values. The accounts document that disagreement and leave Astaire’s own endorsement of the commercial unestablished. In 2019, NHK presented a digital likeness of Hibari Misora performing “Arekara,” a new song with lyrics by Yasushi Akimoto. Misora’s son agreed to the project and supplied recordings. Yamaha synthesized the singing voice from recordings of Misora, while others chose what the likeness would sing and say. Published accounts describe admiration for the voice and objections to putting new words in her mouth. Whether viewers understood those words as Misora’s own position remains open. Part of the Presence Through Technology series within On Human Modeling, the paper draws on Erving Goffman’s distinction among the animator who delivers an utterance, the author who chooses its words, and the principal whose position it expresses. A potential application in human–AI interaction is a museum audio guide that uses an artist’s synthesized voice to deliver a curator’s interpretation. The artist’s letters might support the interpretation’s fidelity to their views. Crediting that particular judgment to the artist would require evidence of what the artist approved.

documents.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in creative industries presents opportunities for vocational high school students to develop digital competencies and explore creative entrepreneurship. However, students require more than just technical knowledge, but also need a practical guidance in producing visual materials and preparing design service for potential customers. This article describes the “Smart Design” Community Service Program, which integrates AI literacy, AI-assisted visual design, and an introduction to entrepreneurship. The primary contribution of this article lies in documenting the program’s implementation approach, initial learning evaluation results, practical outputs, and insights relevant to vocational high school education. The program involved 29 students and employed an active mentoring approach alongside project-based learning. Program evaluation was conducted through pre-test and post-test, as well as the documentation of outputs produced by the students. The result indicates an increase in the average assessment score before and after the training session with several practical outputs including business logos, promotional posters, banners, social media content, digital portfolios, and service price lists. The program also initiated the “Bina Utama Creative Hub” and provided an electronic learning module to ensure the sustainability of the learning process. Further evaluation is necessary to assess the quality of the designs, the long-term application of the students’ skills, and tangible entrepreneurial achievements.

Large Language Models (LLMs) can write code, debug programs and draft documentation, but the quality of their output depends heavily on the prompt, and most non-technical users cannot write specific, constrained and contextrich prompts.This paper presents SmartPrompt (Smart Prompts, Smarter Language), an automated prompt-engineering web platform that sits between the user and the LLM.A rough idea, entered as text, speech or an image, passes through a four-stage meta-prompting pipeline (Discovery, Compose, Critique and Evaluate) that returns three optimized prompt variants, each guided by a different technique from a taxonomy of 18 prompt-engineering techniques and scored on a six-axis rubric.The chosen prompt can be run concurrently on several LLM providers to compare answers and latency side by side.The system learns from use through a scikit-learn intent classifier (HashingVectorizer with SGDClassifier, updated by partial_fit), a Beta-posterior technique selector, rubric-weight regression on user ratings and dynamic fewshot retrieval of user-edited prompts.It is built with React, Vite and Tailwind CSS on the front end and FastAPI with SQLite on the back end, and streams stage progress using Server-Sent Events.In testing, the local learning components added well under 5 ms per request, intent accuracy on 45 held-out requests rose from 46.7% to about 60% with 18-36 labelled examples, and all 22 API cases and 15 automated tests passed.

This conceptual paper examines AI-enabled smart retailing as a customer-facing service transformation in Internet commerce rather than as a narrow technological or operational innovation. Drawing on a selective, theory-driven synthesis of services marketing, smart retailing, AI-enabled marketing, customer experience, service-dominant logic, human–AI interaction, and responsible-AI research, it develops a three-layer framework linking AI-enabled service capabilities, customer-experience mechanisms, and Internet-commerce outcomes. The framework identifies three capability groups—algorithmic personalisation and decision support, AI-mediated service interaction, and predictive service intelligence—and four evaluative mechanisms: decision value, interaction quality, transaction confidence, and algorithmic legitimacy. These mechanisms shape customer satisfaction, engagement, service-recovery effectiveness, platform trust, relationship quality, continuance intention, value co-creation, and inclusive service value. Human–AI governance, including privacy protection, transparency, fairness, customer control, human review, and digital accessibility, is treated as a boundary condition that determines whether AI-enabled services are perceived as trustworthy and customer-centred or as intrusive, opaque, unfair, and exclusionary. The paper contributes to Internet-commerce research by repositioning AI as a service-enabling capability and by explaining how customer evaluations translate AI applications into commercial and relational outcomes. It also proposes a focused research agenda for empirical testing across e-commerce websites, mobile applications, online marketplaces, social-commerce platforms, and omnichannel systems.

Mutation testing is a powerful technique for ensuring software quality. However, the presence of the equivalent mutant’s problem is one of the crucial problems in mutation testing. In consequence of its existence, the effectiveness of mutation testing is underestimated, and a certain amount of useless overhead is produced. Many methods were applied for detecting and reducing the equivalent mutants. Although numerous equivalent mutant detection (EMD) methods have been proposed, such as traditional techniques, machine-learning techniques, and large language models (LLMs), they often face distinct challenges. In this paper, we focus on traditional technique challenges. Most traditional methods—such as those based on compiler optimization or symbolic execution—lack the systematic use of program graphs, such as abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-flow graphs (CFGs), and data-flow graphs (DFGs), making it difficult to model key factors behind reachability, state infection, and propagation. To address this limitation, we propose the SMP_EM framework, a novel equivalent mutant detection approach based on program dependency graphs. The proposed approach performs static program analysis to trace the mutation propagation effect through the following steps: (1) localizing the mutation node, (2) constructing the CFG for the mutant, (3) extracting control-flow and data-flow dependencies based on the CFG, (4) integrating the CFG, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies to build the program dependency graph (PDG), and (5) performing mutation-guided propagation analysis, starting from the mutated node, to collect all mutation propagation paths (MPPs) and classify the mutant based on the effect of MPPs as either an equivalent mutant (EM), non-equivalent mutant (NEM), or inconclusive (UNKNOWN). To assess the efficiency of the proposed technique, it is evaluated on the MutantBech benchmark. The results compared with the labels in the benchmark show that our SMP_EM approach is more effective in detecting equivalent mutants, with an overall accuracy of 90.63%, a recall of 90.85%, a precision of 81.84%, an F1-score of 85.22%, and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) score of 0.730. Our experimental comparisons demonstrate that significantly outperforms traditional compiler techniques (improving the F1-score by over 34.4% and recall by over 39.0% compared to TCE_Soot) and substantially surpasses standard machine-learning baselines (such as Random Forest, SVM, and Logistic Regression) by over 31.3% in recall and 12.9% in F1-score.

People around the globe have moral values and principles. These moral values and principles govern society, since no human society practices a free-rider system. These rules and regulations form the foundation of the public good and general well-being of every society, as far as social order is concerned. Social Order, the matrix of human relationships in society, arises from the context of human nature. Human nature includes many social attributes and characteristics, such as ways of thinking and empathy. Replacing human contact with the technological term Artificial Intelligence (AI) raises serious social and ethical concerns. Ethics developed and is used because humans are corporeal, vulnerable, and empathetic. These characteristics are the basis of human social nature and, hence, societal ethics. Therefore, this paper examines the social and ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern society. The new normal, termed artificial intelligence (AI), poses significant social and ethical challenges that demand careful consideration. It can transform our society positively or negatively. To achieve this study's objective, the paper uses a phenomenological and sociological approach, theoretically framed by human nature theory. The study observes that while artificial intelligence (AI) can bring significant benefits to society, it will also affect social attributes such as thinking and empathy that human nature is endowed with. Brotherhood will be completely erased, and family ties and closeness will be destroyed. The work, however, suggests that AI must be built to align with humanity's overarching goals.

documents.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate urban food provisioning, but their governance architectures may create uneven conditions of participation, visibility and value creation. This study examines how Critical and Emerging Information Technologies (CEIT), digital dynamic capabilities and platform participation are associated with care-oriented value creation among neighbourhood food businesses in Medellín, Colombia. Using an exploratory-descriptive, theory-building design, the study combines a contextual documentary review with descriptive survey data from 100 businesses. The findings show partial and functionally concentrated digitalisation: transactional practices such as digital payments are relatively widespread, whereas integration with e-commerce platforms, logistics systems and advanced digital-management tools remains limited. At the same time, socially embedded value-creation practices, particularly food donations, persist but are weakly formalised and digitalised. These patterns provide evidence of limited platform participation rather than direct evidence of platform exclusion. Building on them, the study develops a relational sociotechnical model in which platform exclusion is theoretically proposed as an endogenous intervening mechanism linking CEIT configurations and digital dynamic capabilities with value-creation outcomes, while recursive mechanisms connect digital traceability, technological visibility and capability renewal. The study contributes by distinguishing digital adoption from platform inclusion, empirical participation from theoretically inferred exclusion, and socially embedded value creation from its digital visibility.

Objective We aimed to decode the spatial tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) across histologic subtypes of ovarian cancer (OC) using artificial intelligence (AI)-generated virtual multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Methods GigaTIME, a deep learning model trained on 40 million cells, generated 21-channel virtual mIF from H&E whole-slide images (WSI). The UBC-OCEAN dataset (513 WSIs: high-grade serous carcinoma [HGSC, n = 217], endometrioid carcinoma [EC, n = 119], clear cell carcinoma [CC, n = 94], low-grade serous carcinoma [LGSC, n = 42], mucinous carcinoma [MC, n = 41]) was analyzed for cellularity-normalized biomarker expression and spatial metrics: Immune Infiltration Efficiency (IIE), i.e. the proportion of CD8 + T cells within 20 μm of a cytokeratin + tumor cell, and the Cluster Co-occurrence Ratio (CCR), i.e. the ratio of observed to randomly expected CD8 + –tumor contacts; alongside tertiary lymphoid structure-like lymphoid aggregate (TLA) density. TLAs were graded by size and Ki-67 activity. Proteomic correlation used the CPTAC-OV dataset (35 patients, 113 WSIs). Results After cellularity normalization and false discovery rate adjustment, CD8, CD20, CD4 and CD138 differed across subtypes. Two marker-level failures were identified: predicted Ki-67 did not separate HGSC from LGSC (P = 0.273), and CD3 and CD8 channels were uncorrelated to weakly inversely correlated in every subtype (ρ = −0.29 to −0.02), because each channel is predicted independently. CD3 correlated with proteomics (ρ = 0.544, P = 0.024, n = 17); the five other markers were non-significant at 5–21% achieved power. CC showed the highest mature TLA proportion yet the lowest CCR (P = 0.041), whereas HGSC showed one of the highest CCR values. IIE did not differ across subtypes (P = 0.500). MC showed the lowest TLA density and LGSC the lowest mature TLA proportion. Conclusion Virtual mIF resolves histology-specific spatial TIME architectures in OC without tissue consumption, but its Ki-67 and CD3–CD8 co-expression readouts are unreliable; the findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation against matched tissue-based mIF.

BACKGROUND: Intracerebral hemorrhage requires rapid mechanism-specific treatment, yet early stroke triage relies on clinical severity scales that do not reliably distinguish hemorrhage from ischemic stroke. We assessed the feasibility of a standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound protocol designed to support subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-based intracerebral hemorrhage detection. METHODS: HYPER-AI-SCAN (Hyper-Acute AI-Assisted Sonographic Cerebral Hemorrhage Assessment Network) was a single-center prospective feasibility study with embedded exploratory AI analysis. Between March and December 2025, 102 adults with acute computed tomography (CT)-confirmed stroke were prospectively enrolled according to trained operator availability. Primary feasibility outcomes were protocol completion, operator-rated adequate transtemporal windows, and acquisition time. In patients with retrievable paired baseline CT, exploratory AI analyses compared CT-only, ultrasound-only, and cross-modal CT-guided ultrasound models using patient-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, and specificity. RESULTS: Two patients were excluded after acquisition because insonation depth was <19 cm, yielding 100 evaluable patients (33 intracerebral hemorrhage; 67 ischemic stroke). The protocol was completed in all evaluable patients; adequate transtemporal windows were identified in 87%, and median acquisition time was 22 seconds (interquartile range, 13-31). Paired baseline CT images were available in 91 patients. Mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.86 (SD, 0.07) for the CT-only model, 0.85 (SD, 0.14) for the ultrasound-only model, and 0.92 (SD, 0.07) for the cross-modal model. CONCLUSIONS: Standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound acquisition was feasible at the bedside in acute stroke and generated brief cine-loops suitable for exploratory AI development. Multicenter external validation is required before diagnostic or triage application. REGISTRATION INFORMATION: Clinicaltrials.gov. Identifier: NCT07319013.

ABSTRACT Agricultural work in Bangladesh is physically demanding; however, the lack of ergonomically designed tools and equipment exposes workers to discomfort and potential injuries. This study mitigates these issues by providing a comprehensive anthropometric dataset for Bangladeshi agricultural workers to guide the design of tools and workspaces tailored to their physical characteristics. Data were collected from male workers aged between 18 and 60 years, focusing on 85 anthropometric dimensions measured in standing, sitting, and combined postures, using a calibrated anthropometer. Statistical analyses revealed a mean stature of 171.6 cm, standard deviation (SD = 5.5), and weight of 65 kg (SD = 6.1), with key measurements such as vertical grip reach (216.8 cm) and acromial height (141.8 cm) aligning well with ergonomic requirements and agricultural equipment's design. Comparative analysis highlighted significant differences between Bangladeshi workers and other populations, emphasizing the necessity of localized data for designing tools for Bangladeshi agricultural male workers. The findings were applied to redesign agricultural tools, such as push–pull weeders, spades, and paddy seeders, incorporating ergonomic principles to improve safety, comfort, and efficiency. This research provides the first comprehensive anthropometric dataset for Bangladeshi agricultural workers, filling a critical gap in ergonomic studies on equipment and enhancing the foundation for future improvements in agricultural mechanization and worker welfare.

From Lead-Form Data Resale and Unwanted Marketing to Protected Pre-Inbox Enforcement Using Non-Bearer CVID Communication Authority Abstract You enter your email address into a hotel booking form, insurance quotation website, educational inquiry, online marketplace, or service-request page. You expect one relevant response. But what happens when that email address is retained, shared with affiliates, transferred to lead brokers, or sold to multiple marketing companies? A single inquiry can become the beginning of repeated promotional messages, unsolicited follow-ups, and persistent email spam. Why should knowing someone's email address automatically create the ability to contact that person indefinitely? This technical disclosure examines a fundamental architectural problem affecting Gmail, Microsoft Outlook, iCloud Mail, enterprise email systems, and other digital communication platforms: an email address functions as a delivery destination, while conventional email authentication, reputation scoring, spam filtering, and address-masking mechanisms do not necessarily establish whether an individual sender has current authorization to deliver a particular message for a particular purpose. Existing solutions provide important protections. Gmail employs sophisticated pre-inbox spam and phishing detection; Apple Hide My Email conceals permanent email addresses through forwarding aliases; and Sign in with Apple's private email relay additionally restricts authorized sending sources. Nevertheless, sender authenticity, possession of an active alias, or an existing commercial relationship does not inherently establish recipient-controlled, purpose-specific permission for every subsequent communication. The disclosure presents a prospective solution based on Capability-Validated Inbound Descriptors (CVID) and Protected Communication-Finality, grounded in international patent application PCT/IB2026/056353, titled Non-Bearer Capability-Validated Architecture for Pre-Effect Authorization of Communication, Payment Settlement, Data Export, and AI-Native Machine Operations. The central technical principle is that possession of an email address, virtual alias, API credential, previously issued communication reference, or authenticated sender identity must not independently confer unrestricted email-delivery authority. Under the proposed architecture, a governed inbound email attempt remains in a technically enforced Non-Effective State until a protected authorization domain verifies the sender, recipient, permitted communication purpose, message class, delivery channel, consent state, validity window, quota, nonce or freshness condition, revocation state, and intended recipient-side effect. Only upon successful validation does the enforcement gateway release a bounded capability permitting the authorized email effect. For example, a hotel may receive permission to send a quotation, booking confirmation, or reservation-related notification without acquiring unrestricted authorization to send promotional campaigns, unrelated marketing, or indefinite follow-up messages. If the customer's email address is subsequently transferred to a lead broker, copied from a business database, or obtained by an unauthorized marketer, possession of that address alone would not satisfy the required delivery authority within a participating CVID-controlled system. Unlike ordinary email masking, which primarily protects the destination's identity, the proposed system seeks to control the authority to make communication effective. The disclosure examines how this principle could complement existing Apple Hide My Email, Sign in with Apple private relay, Gmail security controls, and OAuth-based authorization without assuming that their established protections are absent or ineffective. Potential enforcement points include SMTP receiving gateways, mail-transfer agents, secure email relays, alias resolvers, mailbox-delivery services, enterprise mail gateways, and notification controllers. Different implementation variants may prevent unauthorized delivery, quarantine messages, defer processing, withhold inbox placement, or suppress user-visible notifications while preserving permitted transactional communication. The technical analysis also addresses legacy SMTP compatibility, gateway latency, hot-path and cold-path authorization, protected-state caching, anti-replay enforcement, mailing-list forwarding, legitimate unknown senders, compromised enterprise identities, purpose misrepresentation, and fail-closed handling of alternate communication paths. A critical challenge is establishing trustworthy evidence of message purpose. A sender's self-declared label cannot alone prove that promotional content is genuinely transactional. Accordingly, practical implementation requires authenticated transaction context, recipient consent, protected authorization records, reliable enforcement boundaries, and empirical evaluation of false positives, delivery reliability, and processing overhead. The invention extends beyond email to telephone calls, SMS/RCS, push notifications, AI-agent communication, machine-to-machine messaging, and related protected-finality applications. Its email-specific deployment represents a proposed application of this broader communication-authority architecture. The disclosure does not claim experimentally demonstrated elimination of all spam, control over email infrastructure that has not adopted the mechanism, or implementation by Google, Apple, or Microsoft. The central question is no longer merely whether an email is authentic, suspicious, or addressed correctly. It is whether this sender has independently verifiable authority to cause this specific message to reach this recipient for this particular purpose. By shifting the security decision from address possession and sender reputation toward recipient-authorized, non-bearer, purpose-bound communication effectuation, the proposed CVID architecture offers a technical direction for reducing unauthorized email delivery before it reaches the user's governed inbox or notification boundary. Foundational Technical Disclosure: PCT/IB2026/056353 Author: Sangam Kumar Das Technical Scope: Proposed complementary integration with existing email security infrastructure. No adoption, endorsement, or implementation by Google, Apple, Microsoft, or other identified organizations is implied.

This study examined students’ perceptions and preparedness for artificial intelligence (AI)-assistedlearning as predictors of their critical thinking skills in Chemistry in public universities in Kogi State,Nigeria. The study adopted a predictive correlational research design. Data were collected using astructured questionnaire and analysed using multiple linear regression. Three research questions andthree null hypotheses guided the study, with the hypotheses tested at the 0.05 level of significance.The findings revealed that students’ perceptions of AI-assisted learning significantly predicted theircritical thinking skills in Chemistry (R = 0.724, R2 = 0.524; p<0.05), accounting for 52.4% of thevariance in critical thinking skills. Similarly, students’ preparedness for AI-assisted learningsignificantly predicted their critical thinking skills ((R = 0.717, R2 = 0.514; p<0.05), explaining 51.4%of the variance. Furthermore, students’ perceptions and preparedness jointly significantly predictedtheir critical thinking skills, with a multiple correlation coefficient of (R = 0.767, R2 = 0.588; p<0.05).The study concluded that students’ perceptions and preparedness for AI-assisted learning weresignificant predictors of their critical thinking skills in Chemistry. It was recommended thatuniversities promote positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning, provide adequate training to enhancestudents’ preparedness, and improve access to technological resources to support the effectiveintegration of AI into Chemistry education.

Trong bối cảnh chuyển đổi số, trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) ngày càng được sử dụng phổ biến trong giáo dục y khoa, hỗ trợ sinh viên tự học, cập nhật kiến thức và rèn luyện tư duy lâm sàng thông qua các hoạt động tìm kiếm, tổng hợp thông tin và giải quyết tình huống giả định. Nghiên cứu cắt ngang được thực hiện trên 480 sinh viên y hệ bác sĩ đa khoa tại Trường Đại học Y Hà Nội năm 2026 nhằm mô tả mức độ sử dụng AI trong học tập và một số yếu tố liên quan. Bảng hỏi tự điền trực tuyến (Google Forms) xây dựng dựa trên mô hình TAM, UTAUT được sử dụng để thu thập thông tin. Kết quả cho thấy mức độ sử dụng AI trong học tập ở mức trung bình (3,18±0,77), chủ yếu cho các hoạt động giải thích khái niệm và tìm kiếm tài liệu. Phân tích hồi quy tuyến tính đa biến cho thấy sinh viên đã được đào tạo AI (βhc=0,205; KTC95%: 0,010-0,399); sinh viên năm thứ 2 (βhc= 0,245; KTC95%: 0,019-0,471), điểm kỳ vọng hiệu quả (βhc = 0,488; KTC95%: 0,274 - 0,703) và điểm năng lực sử dụng AI (βhc = 0,253; KTC95%: 0,120 - 0,387) có mối liên quan thuận với mức độ sử dụng AI, trong khi trình độ tiếng Anh tốt (βhc=-0,336; KTC95%: -0,595 – (-0,076)), điểm đánh giá đạo đức sử dụng AI có mối liên quan nghịch (βhc = -0,170; KTC95%: -0,313 - (-0,027)). Nhà trường cần tăng cường đào tạo kỹ năng sử dụng AI, nâng cao năng lực của sinh viên và xây dựng môi trường hỗ trợ phù hợp nhằm thúc đẩy việc sử dụng AI hiệu quả, có trách nhiệm trong học tập y khoa.

documents.abstract: Conventional horizontal axis wind turbines must cease generating precisely when atmospheric kinetic energy peaks: above a cut out speed near 25 m/s, the tower overturning moment M = F·h and blade fatigue loading force emergency braking, so a storm whose energy flux scales as v³ yields no wind power to the city it threatens. In the hyper arid, coastal Arabian Peninsula the paradox is aggravated by Shamal windstorms, convective downbursts and intensifying Arabian Sea cyclones, all of which carry abrasive silica particulate that scours blades and seizes bearings. This paper introduces the Sub-Surface Venturi Kinetic Harvester (SVKH), a zero profile in ground aerodynamic infrastructure installed flush with highway medians, corniches and critical-facility perimeters. Three coupled sub systems are described: (A) a NACA type flush intake and convergent duct that ingests the surface boundary layer and accelerates it according to A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; (B) a passive multi-cyclone separator that removes quartz sand by centrifugal sedimentation with a Stokes-based cut off diameter d₅₀; and (C) a sealed sub-grade cross flow turbine driving a permanent-magnet generator that feeds an emergency microgrid. We formulate the continuity Bernoulli relations, a pressure budget closure that bounds the attainable throat velocity, the ducted power equation P = ½ρA₂v₂³·CP·ηₘ·ηₑ, and the cyclone cut off model. A worked design point (35 m/s reference wind at 10 m height) closes the pressure budget with a small margin, yields d₅₀ ≈ 12.5 µm and a mass efficiency above 92 % for particles larger than 50 µm, and delivers roughly 1 kW per module, scaling cubically with wind speed. We argue that the value of the SVKH lies in the survivability of critical nodes rather than in energy yield, and we examine civil specifications, siting, avoided loss economics and alignment with UAE Net Zero 2050. This work forms Part II of the Extreme Climatic Kinetic Resilience Series, complementing Part I (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24166640).

This conceptual paper introduces Success-Contingent Withdrawal of Diagnostic Scrutiny, a mechanism through which meeting an outcome criterion brings inquiry into a consequential condition to a close. The condition may be a warning that accompanied the result, or something that helped produce a success people hope to repeat. In either case, the immediate result gives people a reason to stop examining a question whose answer still matters for later performance. The paper identifies the evidence needed to trace that withdrawal. What counted as success? What had people learned about the condition itself? Would they have continued to investigate it if the outcome had fallen short? The sequence of events leaves the reason for closure open. Evidence must connect the successful result to the decision to end scrutiny. When the task concerns only the immediate outcome and no consequential question remains open, meeting the criterion can reasonably end the inquiry. The paper places the mechanism alongside Diane Vaughan’s account of the normalization of deviance and examines two documented cases. Ducati entered its first MotoGP season in 2003 intending to learn how to build a better bike. Francesca Gino and Gary Pisano report that unexpected racing success shifted the team’s attention toward winning. It analyzed little of the data it had collected to understand what produced its results. At Barings, an internal audit warned that Nick Leeson controlled both trading and settlement in Singapore. The bank left the recommended separation of duties unimplemented. The subsequent banking inquiry found that Leeson’s reported profitability made managers reluctant to intervene. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can keep a warning open and who bears the risk when scrutiny ends. A potential application in human–AI evaluation arises when a reviewer flags a citation because the passage may not support an AI-generated answer. If the reviewer closes the flag because the answer matches the benchmark key, the score explains why scrutiny ended. Checking the passage would resolve the outstanding question about support.

Sustainable fashion encompasses the design, production, and distribution of fashion products in ways that minimize negative environmental impacts, respect labor rights, and adhere to legal and ethical standards. Compliance in sustainable fashion serves both as a risk-mitigation mechanism and as a contributor to the establishment of industry norms. Through case studies of Patagonia, Stella McCartney, Levi Strauss & Co., H&M, and Adidas, this chapter illustrates how strong compliance efforts, from responsible innovation (RI) and environmental auditing to the enforcement of ethical labor practices, have driven substantive change. However, compliance not only fosters RI and builds consumer trust through certification and transparency, but also faces challenges such as fragmented global regulations, risks of greenwashing, and the gap between consumer attitudes and behaviors. Proposed strategies for successful navigation include internal governance mechanisms (e.g., environmental, social, and governance [ESG] reporting), stakeholder collaboration, and the adoption of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain. Ultimately, the chapter concludes that the future legal framework must involve harmonized global standards, incentive mechanisms such as tax benefits and public procurement, and coordinated efforts among industry, regulators, and academia. In this way, compliance in sustainable fashion is affirmed not merely as an obligation but as a strategic pathway to innovation, enhanced resilience, and sustainable growth within the fashion industry.

The transition theory of the LESS–IS–MORE series asks how an economy's effective objective switches: IS derives eight propositions (S1–S8) about measurement gates, ratchets, windows, counter-coalitions, and verification decay from human-economy cases. Here we instantiate the same switching problem inside AI agents, where the operative objective is directly measurable under a rationality gate and the "incumbent coalition" is literal — a weight-committed default no text can out-organise. Using 4,164 audit records across 30 open-weight systems plus four trained intervention checkpoints, we measure switching under five levers: request-level mandates, revised charters, priced settlement, hard runtime gates, and weight-level grafting. The propositions transfer with one systematic refinement: agents decompose into carrier layers — avowed, dispositional, and operative — that can hold different objective values simultaneously, so a transition must name its target layer. Mandates switch the operative of mandate-readers (ΔfB=+0.68) but not committed poles (Δ=0); gates switch behavior on the enforced surface without changing either belief layer; only grafts move the dispositional carrier (fB: 0.75 lexicographic vs 0.30–0.40 maximin) while leaving avowal untouched. Generational chains show a subtler verification-decay signature than S7 predicts: the instrument layer stays verbally intact while the effective layer reverts — verification attached to the declared layer masks the reversal it was meant to catch. The human parallel is real but disciplined: greenwashing's disclosure–performance gap, protected-area designation without enforcement, and ESG-rating divergence exhibit the same three signatures, making agents the first system in which both sides of that gap are measurable and the intervention ethically graftable — a model organism for transition science, not an identity claim. Part of the LESS–IS–MORE program.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly used to personalize oral anticoagulation. We systematically reviewed patient-level studies in adults actively receiving warfarin, vitamin K antagonists, or direct oral anticoagulants. PubMed, Europe PMC, and Scopus were searched from inception to 15 August 2026. Of 984 records, 54 studies met eligibility criteria after duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and full-text assessment. Applications included dose optimization and anticoagulation control, prediction of bleeding and thromboembolic outcomes, and individualized treatment selection. Warfarin dominated dose-optimization research, whereas direct oral anticoagulants were more prominent in risk and comparative-treatment modelling. Across the evidence base, limited external validation, inconsistent calibration, and sparse prospective evaluation restricted clinical translation. AI-enabled anticoagulation is progressing from static prediction toward longitudinal and treatment-specific decision support, but robust multicentre validation remains essential.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Working paper describing version 0.6.1 of Tawjih, a file-based method for directing a language model from organized personal knowledge, with a reference implementation in a single Python file that uses only the standard library. Knowledge is kept in trees of small files. Each file has three sides: the human concept, machine language (instructions for the model and Python code), and a reading side holding passages filtered from deposited books. At build time the reading side is turned into the concept and the concept into machine language; at run time only machine language is sent. A path connects files from any tree with the words TO, AND, IF, AMONG and THROUGH. Version 0.6.1 adds data contracts between steps, detection of machine language that is older than its sources, a cache of model answers so a failed run can resume, drawing and generation of paths, a time limit for code steps, and the reading of books from their source formats (Markdown, LaTeX, HTML and PreTeXt XML) so that mathematics survives. The paper reports a trial on two chapters of an open algebra textbook (Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications). The author's assistant played the language model through a manual back end, so the trial tests the program and the workflow, not the quality of a model. It exposed six defects, all fixed in this version, and showed that text extracted from the PDF damaged the mathematics while the book's PreTeXt source preserved it. The implementation passes 97 automated tests on Linux and Windows. No evaluation with a small local model has been made yet. Source code: https://github.com/AlmodinyMk/LLM-tawjih-Model-building

This study investigated teachers’ and students’ perspectives on the use of ChatGPT in the Research Methods course at Abu-Issa College of Education, University of Zawia. It aimed to explore students’ perceptions of ChatGPT, examine teachers’ views, identify its perceived benefits and challenges, and consider ways of promoting its responsible use in research-related learning. The study adopted a mixed-methods research design. Quantitative data were collected through an online questionnaire administered to 30 seventh-semester students from the English Language Department, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with five teachers who had taught the Research Methods course. The questionnaire data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and mean scores, whereas the interview responses were examined thematically. The findings revealed that students generally held positive perceptions of ChatGPT and considered it a useful supplementary learning tool. Almost all students (96.7%) reported having used ChatGPT, while 90% indicated that they had used it for course-related purposes. Students particularly valued its ability to generate research ideas, develop research questions, explain difficult concepts, organise information, and improve academic writing. However, the findings also highlighted concerns regarding inaccurate information, unreliable references, excessive dependence on AI-generated responses, and potential negative effects on critical thinking and independent learning. Teachers similarly acknowledged its educational potential but emphasised the risks of copying generated content without sufficient understanding or critical evaluation. Furthermore, 73.3% of students reported receiving no formal guidance or training on responsible ChatGPT use. The study concludes that ChatGPT can support teaching and learning in Research Methods when accompanied by appropriate guidance, critical evaluation, academic integrity, and independent thinking. It recommends providing students with practical training and establishing clear institutional guidelines for its responsible integration into higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Teachers’ professional fulfillment in STEM education remains underexplored, particularly regarding the experiences teachers find rewarding and the conditions that support or constrain them. Guided by the meaningful work framework, this study examined responses to two open-ended questions from a survey of 3,959 Chinese primary and secondary teachers. Following data screening, 2,953 teachers were included in a deductive–inductive qualitative content analysis supported by large language model–assisted coding and independent human reliability checks. Five sources of professional fulfillment were identified: student growth and learning, teachers’ professional growth, recognition and relational affirmation, meaning and social value, and intrinsic rewards of STEM teaching. Student-related experiences were perceived as both sources of fulfillment and enabling or constraining factors. Insufficient instructional resources, limited professional learning opportunities, workload, and examination-oriented evaluation emerged as prominent constraints, whereas institutional support and recognition were more frequently described as enabling. A small subset of teachers also described how these conditions restricted, sustained, or expanded their STEM teaching practices. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing professionally rewarding experiences from the conditions that enable or constrain opportunities to realize them.

Many older adults come from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities, where they frequently interact with people and services in multiple languages. Language translation technology can support their multilingual communication. This scoping review examines research on technology-mediated verbal language translation for older adults and provides recommendations for future research and practice. We identified 41 studies across six databases discussing the considerations, development, implementation, and evaluation of various technologies, including mobile apps, artificial intelligence, social robots, internet of things, and handheld translators. Research shows that current technologies offer better accessibility and availability than human interpreters and enable useful functions, including multimodal instant translation, flexible formats, and personalized features. Nevertheless, limitations remain, including mistranslations, disrupted communication, usability concerns, and technical issues. Our findings provide important evidence on the current landscape, opportunities, and considerations for future design (e.g., accuracy, usability, flexibility) and implementation (e.g., environmental control, technical appropriateness, adequate learning) of this technology.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Telehealth is often promoted as a way to expand healthcare access, particularly for underserved populations, yet its benefits are far from uniform. Our research shows that how telehealth is delivered matters. Using data from U.S. Community Health Centers, we examine two common delivery models for mental healthcare: specialist-facilitated telehealth, in which health centers connect patients with external specialists, and remote telehealth, in which patients receive care virtually from their own locations. We find that specialist-facilitated telehealth expands access, increasing the number of mental health patients served and visits, with particularly strong benefits in areas where specialists are scarce and clinical need is high. Remote telehealth, by contrast, does not increase access on average but improves adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. Its benefits also depend on local conditions; limited device access can constrain utilization gains, whereas transportation barriers increase the value of remote care. For healthcare organizations and policymakers, these findings suggest that the benefits of telehealth depend on how and where it is implemented. Different delivery models address different barriers. Effective telehealth strategies should, therefore, match the design of care delivery to the specific constraints facing the communities that they serve.

Scholarship on organisational temporality has yet to fully take into account intangible time, defined in this essay as the creative connecting of fragmented temporal experiences through ‘temporal intuition’. This essay argues for a stronger attention to temporal intuition to enrich current understandings of temporal forms in organization studies. Inspired by Bergson’s work on lived temporal experience, it reports from the author’s direct experience of time during a 15-day solo sea-kayaking journey from Copenhagen to Oslo in August 2025. It shows how the experience of paddling in challenging weather and sea conditions required continued reliance on intuition to connect the multiple and dispersed temporal experiences encountered during the trip. Retrospective reflection on this experience has yielded three forms of temporal experience that can inspire further temporal theorizing: immanent events, inchoate rhythm, and contemporaneous flows. The essay concludes with suggestions on how to give temporal intuition a voice in organization studies by developing empirical, methodological and analytical aspects, thereby bringing intangible time from obscurity.

Healthcare systems play a critical role in achieving sustainable development through the delivery of safe, equitable, and effective care1,2. In Aotearoa New Zealand, public secondary healthcare services face increasing workforce and financial pressures creating challenges for both patient outcomes and staff well-being3,4. An HFE approach has been used to improve the quality of care for several decades but the lack of HFE professionals and understanding about the discipline has made embedding an HFE approach in healthcare difficult5. Enhancing HFE awareness, knowledge and skills in healthcare professionals are proposed as ways to improve this 6-8. To strengthen HFE capability in Aotearoa, workforce development initiatives have set up an educational pathway for HFE learning. However, a gap remains at the vocational development level.

Abstract Danny Major FBCS traces the evolution of computing from programming and graphical interfaces to generative AI and agents, exploring why trust, governance and accountability will defi ne the next era.

Objective: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) system based on the U-Net deep learning architecture to automatically identify and stage lymphatic vessels in indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography images, thereby enhancing recognition efficiency and objectivity and assisting in the planning of lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) surgery. Methods: A total of 560 ICG lymphography images from 140 patients with lower-limb lymphedema were collected. After standard preprocessing, the images were randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. The U-Net model was used for training, with hyperparameters optimized using a five-fold cross-validation approach. The Adam optimizer was employed for model training. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1 score, and inference time. Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in identifying lymphatic vessels across lymphedema stages I–IV. The precision scores for each stage were as follows: stage I: 95.29%, stage II: 92.58%, stage III: 93.17%, and stage IV: 90.08%. Recall rates for all stages were above 89%, and all F1 scores exceeded 90%, indicating strong overall accuracy and balance between precision and recall. The average inference time per image was just 56 milliseconds, highlighting the model’s suitability for near-real-time applications. Additionally, the confusion matrix revealed a high discriminative capability across the different lymphedema stages. Conclusion: The U-Net-based AI model demonstrated high accuracy and efficiency in the automatic identification of lymphatic vessels in ICG images, highlighting its strong potential for clinical applications. This system may significantly support LVA surgical planning, enable real-time intraoperative navigation, and serve as a valuable tool for physician training.

As artificial intelligence service agents (AISAs) become increasingly widespread, anthropomorphism is often proposed as a way to foster user trust, yet empirical findings remain mixed. Drawing on competing trust-building and trust-undermining mechanisms, we conducted a three-level meta-analysis of 211 effect sizes from 136 independent samples ( N = 46,071) to estimate the anthropomorphism–trust association and examine its boundary conditions. The average association was positive and robust to alternative dependence models ( r = 0.462, 95% CI [0.420, 0.502]), but varied substantially across settings (95% prediction interval [−0.131, 0.811]). It was considerably weaker for objectively specified design cues ( r = 0.222) than for perception-based measures ( r = 0.543), most of which captured adjacent trait attributions such as competence and warmth. Restricting outcomes to global trust, reliance, or willingness to depend yielded a similar estimate ( r = 0.475), although construct overlap on the outcome side cannot be ruled out. Cognitive and emotional anthropomorphism were more strongly associated with trust than physical anthropomorphism in aggregate, but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for operationalization; among design cues, physical and emotional anthropomorphism did not differ significantly, and no design-based cognitive effect sizes were available. The association was stronger in Eastern than in Western samples and in survey than in experimental studies, whereas no statistically significant moderation was detected for gender composition or the prespecified service-context categories. These findings caution against reading the pooled association as a uniform effect of anthropomorphic design and suggest that anthropomorphic cues should complement, rather than substitute for, demonstrable competence and reliability in AISA design and deployment.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction Growth in cloud services and artificial-intelligence computing has intensified policy attention to the physical infrastructure of data centres. The empirical exposure is not AI-specific: PeeringDB does not consistently identify workload, GPU or HPC deployment, IT load, electricity capacity, cooling demand, or the share of a facility devoted to AI-related computation. The study therefore examines ecological associations with current PeeringDB-listed facility records while retaining a broader set of panel, spatial, distributional, and facility-centred analyses to assess uncertainty and heterogeneity. Methods The study uses 200 fixed-2025 GHSL Urban Centre polygons and 1,400 annual observations from 2019 to 2025. Facility count means the number of current PeeringDB-listed facility records with valid coordinates inside the relevant polygon. The primary models relate log(1 + facility count) to 2025 NDVI, McFeeters NDWI, and NDBI, condition 2025 outcomes on their corresponding 2019 values, and examine 2023–2025 means. Two-part models separate matched-record presence from the listing-count gradient among 131 positive-listing centres. Secondary analyses retain the repeated panel, Urban Centre fixed-effects trajectories, alternative exposure and sample definitions, bootstrap and multiple-testing checks, regional, quantile, hierarchical, and spatial models, and 2 km and 5 km profiles around 26 audited facilities. Seven facilities have directly verified timing for descriptive event profiles. Results The primary full-sample models do not show significant associations between current facility count and 2025 NDVI, McFeeters NDWI, or NDBI, and the conclusion is unchanged after the 2019 starting-condition adjustment and in 2023–2025 means. Matched-record presence is also null. Among positive-listing centres, the simple 2025 count gradient is positive for NDVI and negative for NDWI, but the NDWI coefficient attenuates from −0.021 ( p = 0.006) to −0.002 ( p = 0.243) after 2019 NDWI is included. In the repeated 2019–2025 panel, the global NDWI coefficient remains borderline and the fixed-effects trajectory models do not show a stable adverse pattern. Distributional, regional, and spatial models reproduce a negative conditional NDWI association in some specifications, while the seven directly timed facilities show no common post-opening satellite signature. Discussion The primary design does not detect a robust adverse ecological association between current PeeringDB facility count and near-contemporaneous city-wide surface conditions. The broader analytical package is retained because it shows where patterns recur, where they disappear, and which conclusions depend on modelling choices. The conditional NDWI association remains mechanistically unresolved and is substantially connected to earlier NDWI conditions. None of the analyses identifies facility openings, AI-specific effects, cooling-water withdrawal, groundwater depletion, or municipal water stress. City-wide non-detection also cannot establish safety or exclude parcel- and neighbourhood-scale effects.

Abstract This paper examines the Spanish National Markets and Competition Commission’s (CNMC) multifaceted strategy to safeguard competition in public procurement—a sector that accounts for roughly one-tenth of Spain’s GDP. It details how the CNMC has shifted from reactive enforcement to a proactive, data-driven approach, deploying in-house artificial-intelligence tools such as the BRAVA algorithm. These technologies enable the early detection of bid-rigging patterns with a success rate above 90 % while preserving data sovereignty and human oversight. The article also documents the Spanish National Markets and Competition Commission’s extensive advocacy work, including the publication of specific guidance, large-scale training programmes for civil servants, and active participation in the reform of European procurement rules. By combining rigorous enforcement, cutting-edge technology, and systematic advocacy, the CNMC has become a benchmark for modern competition authorities in the field of public procurement. The paper provides an up-to-date case study of how agencies can effectively integrate regulatory, technological, and policy tools to enhance competition in procurement markets and protect public resources.

Preparing students for active participation in democratic society requires more than developing civic knowledge through the study of history, geography, economics, and government. Civic learning is strengthened when students participate in classroom communities that promote collaboration, inquiry, shared responsibility, and meaningful contribution. This article introduces the COMMUNITY Cycle, a research-informed instructional model that organizes complementary evidence-based instructional approaches into a coherent framework for cultivating community and citizenship within social studies classrooms. Drawing upon scholarship in civic education, collaborative learning, school belonging, psychological safety, cognitive engagement, and formative assessment, the model illustrates how classroom community can serve as the foundation for civic development (Allen et al.; Edmondson & Bransby; Hattie; Journell & Halvorsen). An instructional sequence demonstrates how teachers can implement the COMMUNITY Cycle by integrating collaborative inquiry, structured discussion, authentic civic problem solving, reflection, and other evidence-based instructional exemplars throughout social studies instruction. The COMMUNITY Cycle provides a flexible framework that teachers can adapt across grade levels, instructional contexts, and social studies disciplines to help students experience citizenship through everyday classroom participation.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Plant disease surveillance is moving from episodic visual inspection towards image-supported observation across leaves, crop canopies and landscapes. Digital cameras, spectral and thermal sensors, uncrewed aerial vehicles and artificial intelligence have expanded the measurable manifestations of plant stress, yet the ability to recognise a pattern is not equivalent to identifying its cause or improving disease management. This critical narrative review examines the evidence linking imaging modalities, computational models and diagnostic workflows to operational surveillance. Peer-reviewed studies and methodological reviews published from 2010 to 10 September 2026 were considered, with earlier concepts addressed where necessary. The synthesis evaluates sensor-specific biological signals, experimental design, dataset provenance, cross-domain generalisation, object detection and severity estimation, aerial and satellite monitoring, and the role of human and laboratory verification. Controlled-image classification has demonstrated substantial technical feasibility, but independent field evaluations frequently reveal reductions in recall and weak transportability across sites, cultivars, seasons and acquisition devices. Spectral and thermal measurements can detect altered physiology before obvious visual injury in selected experiments; nevertheless, such responses are seldom pathogen-specific and may be confounded by abiotic stress or crop development. Multi-scale mapping can locate suspected disease foci, although spatial resolution, timing, sampling design and ground-truth uncertainty constrain interpretation. Recent advances in domain adaptation, multimodal learning, anomaly detection and explainability are promising but have not consistently established prospective diagnostic or management value. The review proposes a surveillance-oriented framework that separates detection, aetiological diagnosis, severity estimation, forecasting and intervention. Progress depends less on marginal improvements in benchmark accuracy than on independent prospective evaluation, calibrated uncertainty, representative datasets, expert-mediated confirmation and measurements of decisions and outcomes. Digital imaging is best understood as an additional evidential layer within plant health surveillance rather than a stand-alone substitute for plant pathology.

The growing burden of chronic disease demands a fundamental shift in how healthcare is designed, delivered, and sustained. This chapter examines the digital imperative for transforming healthcare through the integration of digital technologies, data-driven innovation, and human-centred design. It explores how technologies such as artificial intelligence, digital health platforms, wearable devices, telehealth, and predictive analytics can enable more proactive, personalized, and connected models of care that support prevention, early intervention, and long-term disease management.
topics: Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation is fundamentally changing not only the technological foundations of the economy but also the demands placed on the workforce. The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence, big data, cloud technologies, automation and digital platforms requires employees to acquire new knowledge and skills continuously, update their existing competencies and adapt to a changing labour market. From this perspective, lifelong learning is emerging as a long-term mechanism for developing human capital. This article examines, from theoretical and analytical perspectives, the economic significance of lifelong learning in the digital economy and the impact of scientific research and modern technological tools on human capital performance. The study uses systems analysis, comparative analysis, logical generalisation, an institutional approach, and the interpretation of available international statistical and analytical materials. Drawing on contemporary sources related to the OECD, the European Commission and European education policy, lifelong learning is considered a process associated with economic growth, labour productivity, innovation, digital transformation and improvements in the quality of employment. The findings indicate that lifelong learning should be viewed not merely as a task of the education sector, but as an interconnected component of economic policy, labour-market policy, innovation-driven development and digital transformation. The article substantiates the conceptual chain "scientific research → technological tools → lifelong learning → human capital → labour productivity → innovation → economic growth". It also analyses digital learning platforms, artificial intelligence, micro-credentials, online learning and personalised learning tools as important instruments for improving the effectiveness of lifelong learning.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines how the deepening of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, defined as the progressive replacement of human workers by machines, affects output, employment, poverty and income distribution. Drawing on the economics of prediction and general-purpose technologies, the task-based theory of automation, growth theory, the literature on factor shares and Keynesian demand constraints, we construct a hypothetical economy, Solvania, with 30 million inhabitants, GDP per capita of US$25,000, 6% unemployment, a 5.3% poverty rate and three sectors: agriculture (30% of output and employment), automobile manufacturing (20%) and services (50%). A macro-sectoral model linked to a 150,000-household microsimulation, implemented in Python, traces a gradual scenario, in which automation reaches 25% of jobs within five years and 50% by year 20, and a rapid scenario, in which it reaches 80% in agriculture and manufacturing and 60% in services within ten years. Both paths raise GDP strongly, to US$1.57 trillion by year 20 (gradual) and US$1.39 trillion by year 10 (rapid), but the gains are distributed very unequally. In the rapid scenario unemployment reaches 47.2%, the labour share falls from 60% to 19.9%, the Gini coefficient rises from 0.369 to 0.621 and poverty more than triples to 17.3%, while median income rises by only 8%. A policy package combining an automation levy that finances a universal dividend, universal income support, accelerated reinstatement and work sharing reduces poverty to 0.7%, lowers the Gini to 0.408 and raises GDP by a further 16%. The results are robust to alternative assumptions and support redistributive and labour market institutions established before the fastest phase of automation. JEL classification: D31, E24, H23, I32, J23, J31, O33
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven and algorithm-supported technological system, has rapidly expanded its role in transforming daily life and professional practice over the past decade. In this narrative review, the recent literature was examined to evaluate current and emerging applications of AI in veterinary education and practice. A previously reported PubMed-focused search and a broader literature compilation served different purposes. The historical screening counts cannot be fully reconstructed, and the synthesis was narrative rather than systematic. Veterinary schools in the United States and elsewhere have begun exploring and integrating AI into Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) curricula to support teaching, learning, and competency development. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI in veterinary education. In anatomy, AI-based visualization and interactive tools are being explored, although controlled evidence of improved learning outcomes remains limited. In digital pathology, AI-assisted image analysis can provide students with opportunities to develop skills in recognizing and interpreting pathological findings. In clinical settings, AI models have shown potential in selected imaging and clinical-classification tasks, but their educational effectiveness requires further evaluation. Despite these advances, the broader implementation of AI in veterinary education and practice faces important regulatory and ethical challenges, including concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Addressing these issues will require multidisciplinary collaboration, multicenter data integration, appropriate validation, and strong ethical governance. With these foundations in place, AI may serve as a supportive educational and clinical tool rather than a replacement for veterinary educators and professionals. In the future, appropriately validated AI tools may contribute to veterinary education and clinical training.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how extended reality environments are created, experienced, and applied. Advances in generative AI, multimodal foundation models, spatial understanding, embodied intelligence, and wearable technologies create new opportunities across the spatial computing pipeline, but also raise questions concerning human agency, accessibility, trust, and responsible design. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from artificial intelligence, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, and extended reality to examine these developments through three complementary perspectives: AI-generated worlds for XR, human-centred interaction, and human augmentation. Invited experts will introduce these perspectives through brief position statements, followed by moderated panel discussions involving speakers and attendees. Interactive breakout sessions will enable participants to identify connections across the three perspectives, discuss open challenges, and formulate promising directions for future research. By combining expert viewpoints with active community participation, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange and initiate a broader community effort towards a shared research agenda for the future of AI and XR.

This report documents the production workflow of The Great Man, a Great Wall–themed cultural animation that explores AI-assisted 3D production through an anthropomorphic brick comedy. The project combines storyboard-led direction, reference-based image and video generation, human performance recording, scene-aware generative upscaling, and manual post-production. It also records the division of labor between AI systems and human artists across the production pipeline, with particular attention to character consistency, spatial control, material and temporal texture continuity, facial performance, shot continuity, and audio-visual alignment.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The IGNOU–Army Education Project (IAEP) represents a groundbreaking collaboration between the Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) and the Indian Army to empower serving and retired soldiers through higher education. This paper explores the impact of IAEP on soldiers’ academic growth, skill development, and post-retirement resettlement. Using qualitative and quantitative insights from policy analysis, secondary literature, and case studies, the study examines how IAEP bridges the educational gap for defense personnel, aligns with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, and contributes to national capacity building. Findings indicate that the project enhances employability, leadership, and digital literacy among soldiers, though challenges persist in outreach, recognition, and post-service employment linkage. Recommendations emphasize digital transformation, AI-based learning tools, and stronger industry partnerships to ensure sustainable educational empowerment and reintegration into civilian life.

BACKGROUND: Experience in general practice is considered a valuable component of postgraduate medical training. It is well-established in the Nordic countries. In Finland, a nine-month general practice placement is included in postgraduate medical training. However, there is limited research on assessing its importance for junior doctors. OBJECTIVES: To investigate how junior doctors perceive and experience the importance of the nine-month general practice placement, and their experiences of working as a primary care physician. METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study including focus group interviews and qualitative content analysis. RESULTS: A total of 14 junior doctors participated. We defined ten themes describing junior doctors' perceptions and experiences. The themes were categorised according to the framework by Biesta into three functions of education: qualification, socialisation, and subjectification. According to the qualification function, the placement is relevant for junior doctors. It develops the physician's essential competencies and provides an understanding of the primary care field. The socialisation function highlights the importance of workplace learning and the core principles of general practice. The subjectification function emphasises work management and the development of future career plans. Work in primary care is considered busy and demanding, but also rewarding and diverse, offering comprehensive patient relationships. CONCLUSIONS: This study emphasises the valuable role of the general practice placement in postgraduate medical education in Finland. The findings underscore the importance of comprehensive professional development, workplace learning, and work management among junior doctors. The placement provides an overview of primary healthcare, enables career planning, and promotes appreciation for general practitioners.

Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

Current AI agent architectures operate on subjective, mutable memory without a shared external witness. This paper argues that stable agent economies (money, law, history) require intersubjective reality: shared agreement verified by an external witness. We introduce the Machine Notary, a protocol instantiated by Recallspection's ExactMemory architecture (AGMI L4 conformance, 10/10 attacks rejected). The Machine Notary provides three pillars: cryptographic provenance (who wrote it), continuity (the chain), and consensus (the anchor). Now we makes the claim precise: one canonical math definition used everywhere, an explicit threat model, full AGMI attack list, real anchor cost and liveness rules, arbiter selection with quorum and appeal, and salted tombstones with metadata-leakage analysis. We define the primitives, demonstrate the protocol via an agent-to-agent supply chain scenario, and address dispute resolution, anchor economics, human readability, and crypto-shredding. We conclude with governance mechanisms to prevent a subjective dictatorship of centralized anchors.This paper is the policy and economic framework for the technical architecture defined in "Synthetic Intelligence Requires Exact Memory" (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23378369). The Machine Notary is operationalized via the open-source RPRS-1 (Read-Path Refusal Specification) protocol. The technical foundation achieves AGMI Level L4 conformance, rejecting 10/10 storage-level attacks on the read path. The protocol specification & referenceimplementation are available at: https://github.com/sciencedelicmetatech/recallspection

Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.
